CALIFORNIA UNIFORM DIRECTED TRUST ACT ('TRUST DIRECTOR' / 'TRUST PROTECTOR') — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · The Morgan Family Revocable Trust

BACKGROUND INFORMATION — TRUST DIRECTOR / ‘TRUST PROTECTOR’ ROLE
I, Pat Morgan, am the settlor of The Morgan Family Revocable Trust, and Jordan Lee is serving, or is proposed to serve, as trustee. This information sheet describes California's statutory framework governing a person who holds authority over some aspect of a trust's administration without serving as trustee — a role a trust instrument itself might label a "trust protector," "trust advisor," "special trustee," or "trust director," and which California's own statute calls a "trust director" holding a "power of direction," under the California Uniform Directed Trust Act, Probate Code §§ 16600-16632. This information sheet is background only: it is not itself a grant of a power of direction to Casey Alex or anyone else, does not appoint Casey Alex to any role, and does not modify The Morgan Family Revocable Trust's terms. Only The Morgan Family Revocable Trust's own instrument — or a document that amends it using whatever method that instrument or California law makes available — actually grants a power of direction or appoints a trust director.

‘TRUST DIRECTOR’ IS CALIFORNIA'S STATUTORY TERM — THE STATUTE ITSELF DOES NOT USE ‘TRUST PROTECTOR’
California codified this role in 2023, effective January 1, 2024, as part of the California Uniform Directed Trust Act, Probate Code §§ 16600-16632. The statute's own text uses the terms "trust director," "power of direction," "directed trust," and "directed trustee" — it does not use the phrase "trust protector" anywhere in its operative sections or in the bill that enacted it. Under the statute, a "trust director" is a person granted a power of direction by the terms of a trust, to the extent that power is exercisable while the person is not serving as trustee, and a person is a trust director under this definition regardless of what label the trust instrument itself gives the role — so a role a specific trust instrument calls a "trust protector" can still be a "trust director" for purposes of this statute, and the statute's default rules described elsewhere in this document can still apply to it, depending on how that instrument actually defines the role's powers.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This chapter governs an arrangement commonly known as a directed trust. (2) In a directed trust, the terms of the trust grant a person other than a trustee a power over some aspect of the trust’s administration. (3) Under this chapter, this power is called a power of direction, the person that holds the power is called a trust director, a trustee that is subject to the power is called a directed trustee, and the trust is a directed trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16600(b) (California Legislative Information text), the Legislature's own description of the arrangement this chapter governs (Probate Code § 16600(b)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  "“Trust director” means a person that is granted a power of direction by the terms of a trust, to the extent the power is exercisable while the person is not serving as a trustee. The person is a trust director whether or not the terms of the trust refer to the person as a trust director and whether or not the person is a beneficiary or settlor of the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16602(g) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of 'trust director' (Probate Code § 16602(g)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory term California uses for this role and how broadly that term reaches — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination that any specific trust instrument's own "trust protector," "trust advisor," or similarly labeled role in fact grants a "power of direction" as the statute defines it. This document does not independently verify that no other operative California statute anywhere uses the phrase "trust protector"; it reports that a search of this specific chapter's text and of the text of the bill that enacted it (2023 Senate Bill 801) did not turn up that phrase. This clause cites two different statutory provisions — § 16600(b) and § 16602(g) — both from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times.

THE SCOPE OF A ‘POWER OF DIRECTION’ — AND WHAT THE STATUTE EXCLUDES FROM IT
A trust instrument may grant a "power of direction" to a trust director, and unless the instrument provides otherwise, a trust director may also exercise any further power appropriate to exercising or not exercising that granted power; where more than one trust director holds a power jointly, the default rule is majority decision, again unless the trust instrument provides otherwise. The statute defines "power of direction" broadly to include a power over the investment, management, or distribution of trust property, or other matters of trust administration — but that definition is not unlimited. The statute expressly excludes several specific powers from its own coverage: a power of appointment; the power to appoint or remove a trustee or trust director; a settlor's own power to revoke the trust; a beneficiary's power over the beneficiary's own beneficial interest; and a power that the trust instrument itself requires to be held in a nonfiduciary capacity to achieve the settlor's federal tax objectives. Because the power to appoint or remove a trustee is expressly excluded, a role that a trust instrument gives only that power — without also granting a power over investment, management, distribution, or some other matter of trust administration — falls outside this statute's own definition of a "power of direction," and the default rules on fiduciary status, trustee compliance, and procedure described elsewhere in this document, which this statute supplies, do not by the statute's own terms reach that power.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Power of direction” means a power over a trust granted to a person by the terms of the trust to the extent the power is exercisable while the person is not serving as a trustee. Power of direction includes a power over the investment, management, or distribution of trust property or other matters of trust administration. The term excludes the powers described in subdivision (a) of Section 16606."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16602(d) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of 'power of direction,' including its cross-reference to the exclusions (Probate Code § 16602(d)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  "(a) Subject to Section 16610, the terms of a trust may grant a power of direction to a trust director. (b) Unless the terms of a trust provide otherwise, a trust director may exercise any further power appropriate to the exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction granted to the trust director pursuant to subdivision (a). (c) Unless the terms of a trust provide otherwise, trust directors with joint powers shall act by majority decision."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16608 (California Legislative Information text), the grant of a power of direction, further powers, and the default majority rule for joint trust directors (Probate Code § 16608) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  "(a) This chapter does not apply to any of the following: (1) A power of appointment. (2) The power to appoint or remove a trustee or trust director. (3) The power of a settlor over a trust, to the extent the settlor has a power to revoke the trust. (4) The power of a beneficiary over a trust, to the extent the exercise or nonexercise of the power affects the beneficial interest of the beneficiary. (5) The power over a trust if both of the following apply: (A) The terms of the trust provide that the power is held in a nonfiduciary capacity. (B) The power is required to be held in a nonfiduciary capacity to achieve the settlor’s tax objectives under the United States Internal Revenue Code of 1986 and regulations issued thereunder."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16606(a) (California Legislative Information text), the specific powers the statute excludes from its own coverage, including the power to appoint or remove a trustee (Probate Code § 16606(a)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual scope and exclusions California's statute states — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination that any specific power granted by any specific trust instrument does or does not fall within this statute's definition of a 'power of direction.' This corrects a natural but imprecise assumption: a role commonly described in general estate-planning practice as including the power to remove or appoint a trustee is not, as to that particular power, governed by this chapter's own fiduciary-status and compliance rules — some other body of California trust law may or may not separately govern the exercise of a power to remove or appoint a trustee held by someone other than the trustee, and this document does not independently research or address what that other law provides. This clause cites two different statutory provisions — § 16608 and § 16602(d), together with the exclusions listed in § 16606(a) — all from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times.

THE TRUST DIRECTOR'S DEFAULT FIDUCIARY STATUS AND STANDARD OF CARE
Unless a trust instrument provides otherwise, a trust director has — in exercising or not exercising a power of direction, or a further power appropriate to it — the same fiduciary duty and liability that a trustee would have in a like position and under similar circumstances: the same standard as a sole trustee if the trust director holds the power individually, or the same standard as a cotrustee if the power is held jointly with a trustee or another trust director. The trust instrument may vary that duty or liability to the same extent it could vary a trustee's duty or liability in a like position — meaning the statute's default fiduciary standard, like much of trustee law generally, is one the trust instrument itself can adjust, not an immovable floor. A separate default carve-out applies to a trust director who is licensed, certified, or otherwise authorized to provide health care in the ordinary course of that person's business or profession: unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, that person has no duty or liability under this statute to the extent they are acting in that health-care capacity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A trust director has the same fiduciary duty and liability in the exercise or nonexercise of the power, if the power is held individually, as a sole trustee in a like position and under similar circumstances or, if the power is held jointly with a trustee or another trust director, as a cotrustee in a like position and under similar circumstances."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16612(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the default fiduciary duty and liability standard for a trust director (Probate Code § 16612(a)(1)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  "The terms of the trust may vary the trust director’s duty or liability to the same extent the terms of the trust could vary the duty or liability of a trustee in a like position and under similar circumstances."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16612(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), the trust instrument's ability to vary that duty or liability (Probate Code § 16612(a)(2)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  "Unless the terms of a trust provide otherwise, if a trust director is licensed, certified, or otherwise authorized or permitted by law other than this chapter to provide health care in the ordinary course of the trust director’s business or practice of a profession, to the extent the trust director acts in that capacity, the trust director has no duty or liability under this chapter."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16612(b) (California Legislative Information text), the default carve-out for a trust director acting in a licensed health-care capacity (Probate Code § 16612(b)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default fiduciary standard California's statute states for a trust director — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination of any specific trust director's actual liability in any specific circumstance. The statute's default standard is expressly variable by the trust instrument in both directions — it can be raised, lowered, or otherwise reshaped to the same extent a trustee's own duty or liability could be — so this clause states only the default that applies absent a contrary instrument provision, not what a specific instrument's own terms actually provide. This clause cites three different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 16612 (subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(2), and (b)), all from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times.

HOW A TRUST DIRECTOR'S POWER RELATES TO THE TRUSTEE'S OWN DUTIES
Where a trust instrument grants a power of direction to a trust director, the statute also addresses how the trustee — called a "directed trustee" once subject to that power — must respond to it. Subject to one specific exception, a directed trustee must take reasonable action to comply with a trust director's exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction, and, by default, is not liable for taking that action. The exception: a directed trustee must not comply with a trust director's exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction to the extent that complying would itself amount to willful misconduct by the trustee. Separately, the statute imposes a default, reciprocal information-sharing duty: a trustee must provide a trust director, and a trust director must provide a trustee or another trust director, with information that is reasonably related both to that person's own powers or duties and to the recipient's powers or duties.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Subject to subdivision (b), a directed trustee shall take reasonable action to comply with a trust director’s exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction or further power under subdivision (b) of Section 16608, and the trustee is not liable for the action."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16614(a) (California Legislative Information text), the default rule that a directed trustee must comply, and is not liable for complying (Probate Code § 16614(a)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  "(b) A directed trustee shall not comply with a trust director’s exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction or further power under subdivision (b) of Section 16608 to the extent that, by complying, the trustee would engage in willful misconduct."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16614(b) (California Legislative Information text), the exception where compliance would itself be willful misconduct (Probate Code § 16614(b)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  "(a) Subject to Section 16618, a trustee shall provide information to a trust director to the extent the information is reasonably related both to the powers or duties of the trustee and the powers or duties of the trust director. (b) Subject to Section 16618, a trust director shall provide information to a trustee or another trust director to the extent the information is reasonably related both to the powers or duties of the trust director and the powers or duties of the trustee or other trust director."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16616(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the reciprocal default duty to share information reasonably related to both persons' powers or duties (Probate Code § 16616(a)-(b)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's statute addresses the relationship between a trust director's power and a directed trustee's own duties — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination of any specific trustee's or trust director's actual compliance obligations in any specific circumstance. This document does not address several related default rules in the same chapter that this research did not develop into their own clauses, including the default rule that neither a trustee nor a trust director has a duty to monitor the other or to volunteer advice about how the other might have acted differently (§ 16618), the parallel rule allowing similar relief between cotrustees outside the directed-trust context (§ 16620), the limitation period and available defenses for a breach-of-trust action against a trust director (§§ 16622, 16624), or personal jurisdiction over a trust director who accepts appointment (§ 16626). This clause cites two different statutory sections — § 16614 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) and § 16616 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) — both from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times.

DEFAULT PROCEDURAL RULES — ACCEPTANCE, BOND, COMPENSATION, RESIGNATION, VACANCY, AND WHEN THE STATUTE APPLIES
Unless a trust instrument provides otherwise, the same statutory rules that apply to a trustee's acceptance of office, the giving of a bond to secure performance, reasonable compensation, resignation or removal, and filling a vacancy in office also apply by default to a trust director. This means a trust instrument that appoints a trust director without separately addressing these mechanics can, by default, fall back on the same statutory framework California's Probate Code already supplies for a trustee in each of those areas. Separately, the statute itself states when it applies at all: it reaches a trust, whenever created, that has its principal place of administration in California, and for a trust created before January 1, 2024, the statute applies only to a decision or action occurring on or after that date — meaning a trust created earlier is not retroactively subject to this statute's rules for decisions or actions that occurred before its effective date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Unless the terms of a trust provide otherwise, the rules applicable to a trustee apply to a trust director regarding all of the following matters: (a) Acceptance under Sections 15600 and 15601. (b) Giving of a bond to secure performance under Section 15602. (c) Reasonable compensation under Section 15681. (d) Resignation or removal under Article 3 (commencing with Section 15640) of Chapter 1. (e) Vacancy and appointment of a successor under Section 15660."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16628 (California Legislative Information text), the default rules that apply to a trust director by cross-reference to trustee rules on acceptance, bond, compensation, resignation, and vacancy (Probate Code § 16628) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  "(a) This chapter applies to a trust, whenever created, that has its principal place of administration in this state, subject to all of the following rules: (1) If the trust was created before January 1, 2024, this chapter applies only to a decision or action occurring on or after that date. (2) If the principal place of administration of the trust is changed to this state on or after January 1, 2024, this chapter applies only to a decision or action occurring on or after the date of the change."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16604(a) (California Legislative Information text), when the statute applies, including its non-retroactive effect for a trust created before January 1, 2024 (Probate Code § 16604(a)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&division=9.&title=&part=4.&chapter=6.&article=)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default procedural rules and applicability date California's statute states for a trust director — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination of whether a specific trust's principal place of administration is, in fact, California. This document does not independently quote or address the individual trustee-focused statutory sections that § 16628 cross-references (Probate Code §§ 15600, 15601, 15602, 15681, and the resignation, removal, and vacancy provisions beginning at § 15640 and at § 15660) — some of those same provisions are addressed in a different clause elsewhere in this corpus, in the context of a trustee rather than a trust director, and are not re-quoted here. This clause cites two different statutory sections — § 16628 and § 16604(a) — both from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times.

SIGNATURE AND RECORD BLOCK — TRUST DIRECTOR BACKGROUND INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 5, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Pat Morgan: ☐ _________________________

expectedJSON.body: Where a trust instrument grants a power of direction to a trust director, the statute also addresses how the trustee — called a "directed trustee" once subject to that power — must respond to it. Subject to one specific exception, a directed trustee must take reasonable action to comply with a trust director's exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction, and, by default, is not liable for taking that action. The exception: a directed trustee must not comply with a trust director's exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction to the extent that complying would itself amount to willful misconduct by the trustee. Separately, the statute imposes a default, reciprocal information-sharing duty: a trustee must provide a trust director, and a trust director must provide a trustee or another trust director, with information that is reasonably related both to that person's own powers or duties and to the recipient's powers or duties.

expectedJSON.body: Unless a trust instrument provides otherwise, the same statutory rules that apply to a trustee's acceptance of office, the giving of a bond to secure performance, reasonable compensation, resignation or removal, and filling a vacancy in office also apply by default to a trust director. This means a trust instrument that appoints a trust director without separately addressing these mechanics can, by default, fall back on the same statutory framework California's Probate Code already supplies for a trustee in each of those areas. Separately, the statute itself states when it applies at all: it reaches a trust, whenever created, that has its principal place of administration in California, and for a trust created before January 1, 2024, the statute applies only to a decision or action occurring on or after that date — meaning a trust created earlier is not retroactively subject to this statute's rules for decisions or actions that occurred before its effective date.
